method: ENSO fingerprint per grid. ENSO year y = event peaking Nov(y)-Jan(y+1); El Nino if ONI NDJ(y) >= +0.5, La Nina if <= -0.5, otherwise neutral (NOAA ONI). basin_precip: GPCP v2.3 monthly rainfall (NASA GSFC / GEWEX satellite-gauge merge, 2.5 deg, 1979 onward) at capacity-weighted points near each grid's hydro plants (WRI GPPD); NASA POWER MERRA-2 rainfall is computed the same way as a cross-check. Each year's window total is divided by its centred 11-year running median (removes drift and decadal swings). Two windows are tested: the Oct-Sep water year and the climatologically wettest 6 months; effect = % difference of mean rainfall in El Nino (La Nina) years vs neutral years; the window with the larger effect is kept per phase and the 10,000-shuffle permutation test repeats that choice in every shuffle (corrects for cherry-picking). hydro_generation: Ember monthly hydro TWh per water year, linearly detrended, same composite (low confidence; primary only with >= 10 water years, >= 3 events per phase and >= 4 neutral years). reservoir_level (Zambia, Zimbabwe): G-REALM Kariba level rise from Oct-Nov(y) to Jun-Jul(y+1), tested on the difference in metres. Loser in a phase if effect <= -5% with permutation p < 0.1 on the primary variable. Two-sided p-values.

summary.field_significance_note: If ENSO had no effect, about 2.4 of 48 grids would pass the loser test in each phase by chance (p<0.1, negative sign). We find 12 El Nino losers and 1 La Nina losers. Per-country Benjamini-Hochberg q-values are in el_nino_q / la_nina_q.
summary.strong_el_nino_note: Exploratory: basin rainfall in the 5 strong El Ninos (1982, 1997, 2009, 2015, 2023) vs neutral years, on the El Nino window; not used for the exposure class.
summary.scope_note: Totals cover the 48 hydro-dependent countries; Sichuan is reported separately (part of China). GW is installed hydro capacity from Ember (latest year; GPPD where Ember has none).
summary.headline: 58 GW of hydropower sits in 12 grids that lose output under El Nino (6 GW in 1 grids lose under La Nina), and extreme El Ninos are projected to come about twice as often.
summary.headline_robust: 54 GW of hydropower sits in 9 grids that lose output under El Nino in both the full record and the 1981-2019 check, and extreme El Ninos are projected to come about twice as often.

outlook.summary: El Niño continues to strengthen, with a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely through January-March 2027 (remaining greater than a 79% chance).

cpc.synopsis: El Niño continues to strengthen, with a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely through January-March 2027 (remaining greater than a 79% chance).
cpc.historic_event_text: Chances for a historic event exceeding previous El Niños dating back to 1950 (+2.5°C or more for a 3-month RONI value ) are now ~60% for the October-December and November-January periods

geos.note: GEOS-S2S ensemble-mean Nino-3.4 SST anomaly (C), 3-month seasons from the init month

la_nina_after_strong_el_nino.text: Since 1950, 4 of 8 strong El Ninos (ONI NDJ >= 1.5) were followed by La Nina conditions the next winter (ONI NDJ <= -0.5).

projections.text: Extreme El Nino events are projected to roughly double in frequency under greenhouse warming, from about one every 20 years to about one every 10 years (Cai et al. 2014, 20 CMIP models). The increase continues for about a century even after global warming is stabilised at 1.5 C (Wang et al. 2017). Grids that lose hydropower under El Nino therefore face a structural, not only a seasonal, risk.

refs.title: Cai et al. 2014, Increasing frequency of extreme El Nino events due to greenhouse warming, Nature Climate Change 4, 111-116
NOAA PMEL: Frequency of extreme El Ninos to double in the 21st century
Wang et al. 2017, Continued increase of extreme El Nino frequency long after 1.5 C warming stabilization, Nature Climate Change 7, 568-572
Ng, Turner & Galelli 2017, Influence of El Nino Southern Oscillation on global hydropower production, Environmental Research Letters 12, 034010

enso_years.definition: ONI NDJ(y) >= 0.5 El Nino, <= -0.5 La Nina (years from 1979)

context.literature: Ng, Turner & Galelli 2017: more than a third of 1,593 simulated dams show significant annual production anomalies in at least one ENSO phase; effects are strong regionally and partly cancel globally; reservoirs dampen them.
context.both_phases: Both phases matter: El Nino 2023/24 drained Lake Kariba; Brazil's 2021 hydro crisis happened under La Nina.

robustness_1981_2019.description: Primary variable recomputed on water years 1981/82-2019/20 only (ENSO years 1981-2019), excluding 2020 onward because a GPCP drift/break after 2019-2020 is suspected over the Zambezi (2020/21 and 2021/22 read dry although Kariba rose ~3.2 m in 2020/21). Rainfall baselines (11-yr running median) are rebuilt from in-scope years only. Primary classes are kept; countries whose class changes are marked robust=false.

limitations: Few events: about 16 El Nino and 17 La Nina years since 1979 for rainfall, only about 13 neutral years as the baseline, and only 2-5 events per phase in the Ember generation records (mostly 2015/2019 onward). Effect sizes are noisy; with 48 grids and p<0.1, about 2-3 grids per phase would pass by chance (see BH q-values).

Rainfall is a proxy for hydropower: reservoirs buffer one bad season (Ng et al. 2017 found production anomalies smaller than inflow anomalies), and snowmelt, glaciers and upstream catchments are not captured.

Rainfall is sampled near the largest plants (GPCP 2.5 deg cells), not over the full upstream catchment (e.g. Namibia's Ruacana is fed from Angola; Tajikistan's Vakhsh from high-mountain snow). Small or steep basins (Andes, Balkans, Himalaya) are poorly resolved at 2.5 deg.

GPCP and MERRA-2 disagree in places; MERRA-2 point rainfall shows discontinuities (e.g. Colombia 2007-08 and 2021, a doubling of Vietnam rainfall from the 1980s to the 2010s), which is why GPCP is primary.

Non-stationarity: ENSO teleconnections vary between decades and between El Nino flavours (Eastern vs Central Pacific); a historical fingerprint does not guarantee the response of the 2026/27 event. The 11-year running-median baseline removes slow trends but also part of genuine decadal variability.
Power-plant locations come from WRI GPPD v1.3 (2021); newer plants are missing.
Kariba level is managed (releases, allocation rules), so it mixes climate and operating decisions.
Strong-El-Nino effects rest on 5 events (1982, 1997, 2009, 2015, 2023) and are exploratory.

Sensitivity to the record period: rerunning on water years 1981/82-2019/20 (dropping years with a suspected GPCP break) changes the class of MOZ (el_nino_loser -> neutral), GTM (el_nino_loser -> neutral), GIN (neutral -> la_nina_loser), LVA (neutral -> el_nino_loser), MWI (el_nino_loser -> neutral); these are marked robust=false and kept at their full-record class.
notes: Southern Brazil (GPPD plants south of 23 S) and Uruguay are computed for validation only; they are not in the 48-country list.
